sentences.text: The animal belongs to the genus Yutyrannus, a name combining the Chinese word for feather and the Greek word for tyrant.
Phylogenetic analyses consistently place Yutyrannus within the group Tyrannosauroidea, specifically in the parent group Proceratosauridae.
Three fossils discovered in Liaoning Province represent the largest dinosaur specimens preserving direct evidence of feathers.
The largest known specimen is estimated to be 10 meters long and weigh about 1414 kilograms.
The preserved feathers were long, reaching up to 20 centimeters, and filamentous.
A 2023 study estimated the bite force at 2,405 Newtons (540 pounds-force).
The genus was described by Xu and colleagues in 2012, who named and described Yutyrannus huali.
Researchers suggest the feathers may have covered the whole body to regulate temperature in a climate with an average annual temperature of 10 degrees Celsius.
During growth, the skull became more robust and deeper.
A 2018 study indicates Yutyrannus had a simple hyoid structure and a flat tongue like a crocodile.
Xu Xing speculated that Yutyrannus may have hunted sauropods based on sauropod material found in the same quarry.

Yutyrannus lived during the Early Cretaceous in what is now northeastern China, while other age estimates suggest it originated from the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Asia.
Age estimates suggest Yutyrannus originated from the Lujiatun or Jianshangou beds of the Yixian Formation.
Some researchers previously hypothesized that the structures might be ancestral filamentous structures rather than true feathers.
